nameStory: Olencira praegustator doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists stick with its Latin moniker. The genus name 'Olencira' comes from Greek roots, while 'praegustator' means 'taster' or 'one who tastes first' - a fitting name for a parasite that literally feeds on its host's bodily fluids. Think of it as nature's unwelcome food critic!
description: This is a fish isopod, a type of crustacean parasite that looks like a flattened pill bug but lives attached to fish. These small, oval-shaped creatures are typically pale or translucent with a segmented body that's wider than it is tall. Adults reach about half an inch long and have a distinctly flattened appearance that helps them cling tightly to their fish hosts. [Note: Limited information available for this rare species - only one recorded observation in New England]

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Distinctly flattened and oval, like a tiny pancake with segments, much wider than thick when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Attachment location
idTips.description: Found firmly attached to the gills, mouth, or body surface of marine fish - won't come off easily if touched

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Pale whitish to translucent appearance, sometimes with a slight pinkish tinge from blood feeding

idTips.label: Legs
idTips.description: Seven pairs of small, hooked legs that feel rough and grippy when handling the host fish

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About the size of a large pea or small grape, roughly half an inch long when fully grown

habitat: Found in New England's coastal marine waters, attached to various fish species. Look for them when cleaning fresh-caught fish from rocky shores, estuaries, or deeper offshore waters. They prefer the protected areas around fish gills and mouth cavities where water flow provides oxygen while they feed.

seasonality.spring: May be found on fish caught in warming coastal waters as fish become more active and parasites resume feeding and reproduction.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for observing these parasites on fish caught from New England waters, as warmer temperatures increase both fish and parasite activity.
seasonality.fall: Still active on fish hosts as waters remain relatively warm, though fish populations may be shifting toward deeper or southern waters.
seasonality.winter: Less commonly encountered as many fish species move to deeper waters or migrate, though parasites remain attached to their hosts year-round.

funFact: These parasites can actually change the behavior of their fish hosts, making them swim differently and sometimes even affecting their ability to escape predators - essentially turning fish into zombie-like creatures under parasitic control!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other fish isopods in the family Cymothoidae, but the specific identification often requires microscopic examination. Remember: if it's flat, attached to a fish, and looks like a weird pill bug, it's definitely some kind of fish isopod even if the exact species is hard to determine.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their somewhat disturbing appearance and lifestyle, fish isopods like this one are a normal part of marine ecosystems and don't pose any threat to humans. Finding them on fish is actually a sign of a healthy marine environment with active food webs.
compareHints: Since this appears to be the only Olencira species recorded in New England waters, comparison must be made with other fish isopods in the Cymothoidae family. This species differs from more common fish isopods by its specific size, attachment preferences, and the particular fish species it targets.
